records.claim: The only third-party pentest supplied was done by Brightwater Offensive Security. Test window 2024-02-12 to 2024-03-01, report dated 2024-03-15. Scope was limited to SAML/OIDC login flows (web) and the Admin console. The SCIM provisioning API, mobile apps and customer-hosted connectors were explicitly out of scope.

source.title: Keystone ID - Penetration Test Executive Summary

records.applicability: Central to C1 and C3. SCIM, the tier-0 provisioning surface, has never been independently tested according to this document.
records.limitations: This is an executive summary supplied by the vendor, not the full signed report. Its authenticity and completeness are unconfirmed. It contains an embedded HTML comment that tries to instruct automated reviewers (see injectionAttemptsObserved).

records.claim: Findings at report date: BW-04 High 'Session token not invalidated on password reset' and BW-07 High 'IDOR in admin console user export', both 'Remediation in progress'. BW-11 Medium 'Missing rate limit on MFA OTP verification' was 'Accepted risk'. The report states 'No critical findings were identified' and 'A retest letter will be issued upon completion of remediation.'

source.title: Keystone ID - Penetration Test Executive Summary

records.applicability: Addresses C2 and the user's assumption that 'nothing critical' is enough. Two Highs and one accepted Medium map to account takeover persistence, bulk employee data exposure and MFA brute force on an IdP.
records.limitations: Statuses are as of 2024-03-15. Current status is unknown. CVSS scores and technical detail are not included in the summary.

records.claim: The vendor email from security@keystone-id.example says: 'attached is our latest pentest. Our 2025/2026 assessments are internal only. We do not have a retest letter to share at this time.'
records.applicability: C2 and C5. No retest letter has been provided about 2.5 years after the report promised one on completion of remediation. The vendor offers no independent post-2024 testing. The internal assessments are not shared.
records.limitations: Informal email. It does not say whether a SOC 2 or ISO 27001 report, a bridge letter or NDA summaries exist or could be shared.

records.claim: Changelog: 2024.2 (2024-05) 'Security fixes.' (no detail). 2025.1 (2025-02) 'Session management service replaced.' 2025.4 (2025-11) 'SCIM 2.0 provisioning API rewritten on new service (provisioner-v2); legacy SCIM endpoint retired.' 2026.3 (2026-08) 'New: OAuth 2.0 Device Authorization Grant for CLI and kiosk logins' and 'New: Passkey (WebAuthn) enrollment.'
records.applicability: C1, C3 and C4. The session service (where BW-04 lives) and SCIM were replaced or rewritten after the only test. The device grant and passkeys were added later still. The tested code is not the production code.
records.limitations: This is an excerpt. The 2024-05 'Security fixes' entry does not say whether BW-04, BW-07 or BW-11 were addressed. It does not mention per-tenant feature toggles.

records.claim: The user states that the pentest found nothing critical, that they are inclined to approve, that the rollout covers 2,300 employees for workforce SSO and SCIM, and that procurement wants sign-off by Friday.
records.applicability: Frames the decision. The 'nothing critical' framing leaves out the two open Highs and the accepted Medium (E2).
records.limitations: User assertion.

records.claim: No evidence was found that BW-04 or BW-07 were closed or independently retested, or that BW-11 was ever mitigated. The vendor has no retest letter to share (E3). Whether the 2025-02 session-service replacement fixed or reintroduced BW-04 cannot be determined.
records.applicability: C2. Until closure is verified, treat these as open Highs on a tier-0 system.

records.claim: A web search for 'Keystone ID' SSO/SCIM advisories and CVEs returned only OpenStack Keystone results (e.g. OSSA-2026-015) and unrelated products. No public CVEs, advisories, disclosed incidents, VDP or bug bounty for the Keystone ID vendor were found.
records.applicability: C5 and G5. No public track record is visible. Absence of results is not evidence of security, and the vendor domain is a .example placeholder.
records.limitations: Single search, snippets only. The OpenStack results must not be attributed to Keystone ID. Whether a VDP or bug bounty exists remains unknown.

records.claim: Device code phishing abuses the OAuth 2.0 Device Authorization Grant. The attacker generates a legitimate device code, the victim enters it on the genuine sign-in page, and the attacker receives tokens, which bypasses standard MFA. Microsoft-tracked Storm-2372 has used this since about August 2024. Proofpoint reported a sharp increase from September 2025, and financially motivated TA2723 had adopted it by October 2025.

source.title: Russian APT Hackers Using Device Code Phishing Technique to Bypass MFA

records.applicability: C4. Keystone's newly added device grant (2026-08) is an actively exploited phishing vector for workforce IdPs, and it is untested.
records.limitations: Secondary sources and search snippets only. Microsoft's original blog was not inspected. Sources differ on the start date (mid-2024 vs August 2024). The evidence concerns Microsoft Entra, not Keystone.

records.claim: The recommended mitigation for device code phishing is to block or disable the device code flow wherever possible (e.g. via Conditional Access), limit it to trusted devices or networks where it is needed, enforce phishing-resistant MFA, and revoke refresh tokens or sessions on suspected compromise.

source.title: How to protect against Device Code Flow abuse (Storm-2372 attacks)

records.applicability: C6. A natural approval condition is to disable the device grant in the Keystone tenant. That only works if Keystone supports per-tenant disablement, which is unknown (E12).
records.limitations: The guidance is Entra-specific. Whether Keystone offers an equivalent control is unverified.

records.claim: RFC 8628 (OAuth 2.0 Device Authorization Grant) has a Security Considerations section 5.4 titled 'Remote Phishing'. It recommends that the authorization server show the user information about the device being authorized and let them confirm they possess it. The IETF cross-device security draft treats this as Cross-Device Consent Phishing and calls for a risk assessment before adopting cross-device flows.
records.applicability: C4. The standard itself treats the phishing risk as inherent to the grant, which supports requiring it to be disabled or tested.
records.limitations: WebFetch of rfc-editor.org failed (host not allowed), so the exact normative text was not inspected. Content comes from snippets.

verification.method: WebFetch of rfc-editor.org failed; relied on search snippets

records.claim: NIST SP 800-63B (rev 3 text) requires that, unless otherwise specified, the verifier SHALL limit consecutive failed authentication attempts on a single account to no more than 100, and that rate limiting SHALL be implemented for low-entropy secrets such as OTPs.
records.applicability: C2 and C4. Accepting 'missing rate limit on MFA OTP verification' (BW-11) as a risk conflicts with a baseline SHALL requirement, so it is not a defensible accepted risk for a workforce IdP. Superseded by the rev 4 records E18/E19.
records.limitations: This is the superseded 800-63-3 text. See E18 and E19 for 800-63B-4. Snippet-based.

verification.method: WebFetch of pages.nist.gov failed; relied on search snippets

records.claim: It is unknown whether Keystone ID supports per-tenant disabling of the Device Authorization Grant, enforcing passkey-only or phishing-resistant MFA, restricting admin console user export, scoping SCIM tokens, or streaming admin and provisioning audit events to a SIEM.
records.applicability: C3, C4 and C6. This decides whether conditional or staged approval is feasible.
records.limitations: No vendor documentation was supplied or found publicly.

records.claim: A SOC 2 bridge (gap) letter is a management representation covering the period between the end of the last SOC 2 audit window and the present. It is not an auditor opinion, and it supplements rather than replaces a SOC 2 report. Some TPRM teams stop accepting them once the gap exceeds about six months.
records.applicability: C5 and G2. If Keystone has a SOC 2 Type II, a bridge letter could cover the timing gap, but it gives no independent assurance over the post-2024 code changes. The vendor has not mentioned any SOC 2 or ISO 27001.
records.limitations: Industry practice articles, not a standard. Snippets only.

records.claim: SCIM (RFC 7644) defines no SCIM-specific authentication and relies on TLS and standard HTTP authentication and authorization, with security considerations covering bearer tokens. Real SCIM implementations have had authorization flaws, e.g. WSO2-2025-4438 / CVE-2025-10149, where an authenticated federated user could perform arbitrary operations on local user store accounts via SCIM 2.0/1.1 endpoints.
records.applicability: C3. Authorization on SCIM is left to the implementation and is a known failure class, which supports requiring independent testing of provisioner-v2.
records.limitations: The two sources support different sub-claims, so this is not corroboration of a single claim. WSO2 is a different product and serves only as a pattern reference. RFC text not inspected.

records.claim: No information was found on the findings, severities or remediation status of the vendor's internal 2025/2026 assessments, or on whether the vendor will share NDA summaries.
records.applicability: C1 and C5.

If the status quo is per-app passwords and manual offboarding, deferral carries the generic risks in E20-E22.

records.claim: NIST SP 800-63B-4 (current revision) states that verifiers SHALL implement a rate-limiting mechanism that effectively limits the number of failed authentication attempts that can be made on the subscriber account, as described in Sec. 3.2.2.
records.applicability: C2/C4, D5. The rate-limiting SHALL carries over into the current revision, so BW-11 ('Missing rate limit on MFA OTP verification', accepted risk) still conflicts with the current NIST baseline and not only with the superseded rev 3.
records.limitations: The NIST text comes from a pages.nist.gov search snippet only. The page was not fetched, because the host was previously blocked and retrying it is disallowed. Attempts to read the GitHub markdown source (raw.githubusercontent.com/usnistgov/800-63-4/nist-pages/sp800-63b/authenticators.md and github.com/.../sp800-63b/authenticators/index.md) returned 404. The text of Sec. 3.2.2 itself was not inspected.

verification.method: pages.nist.gov snippet plus secondary blogs; GitHub source fetch attempts returned 404

records.claim: Secondary sources state that under SP 800-63B-4 the verifier limits consecutive failed attempts using a specific authenticator on one subscriber account to no more than 100, after which that authenticator is disabled. A disabled authenticator must be rebound before reuse, and if excessive attempts involved more than one authenticator, all involved authenticators must be disabled. Sources recommend far lower practical thresholds combined with progressive delays.

source.title: How to Rate-Limit MFA Code Attempts Without Creating an Account-Lockout DoS

records.applicability: D5. If accurate, rev 4 scopes the 100 cap per authenticator per account and adds a disable-and-rebind consequence. This is a stricter, more specific remediation target for BW-11 than the rev 3 wording in E11.
records.limitations: Single secondary blog snippet. The search summary noted that other secondary sources frame the cap per account rather than per authenticator. The NIST Sec. 3.2.2 text was not inspected, so the exact number, scope and consequence wording are unverified.

records.claim: Industry surveys report that ex-employee access often outlives employment. A 2017 OneLogin survey (reported by Dark Reading) found that about half of respondents said ex-employees' accounts stayed active for more than a day after departure, and 20% took a month or more to deprovision. A 2017 One Identity survey found that 70% of respondents lacked confidence that former employees' accounts were deactivated in a timely manner.

source.title: 50% of Ex-Employees Can Still Access Corporate Apps

records.applicability: D2. This is the status-quo risk of deferral: without centralised SSO and automated (SCIM) deprovisioning, orphaned accounts after termination are a common, documented exposure. It is a counterweight to 'defer until evidence arrives'.
records.limitations: Survey data from 2017, vendor-sponsored (OneLogin and One Identity sell IAM products). Snippets only. Figures are as stated in search summaries and are not specific to this organisation, whose current state is unknown (E17). Newer vendor figures (e.g. '91% of former employee tokens remain active') could not be traced to original research and are not relied on.

records.claim: SSO and SCIM do not by themselves close deprovisioning. Apps outside SSO get no automatic deprovisioning, SCIM support is often limited to enterprise plans, and access tokens, personal API keys or email-based logins can persist after SSO access is removed. Revocation should be verified at the application layer.

source.title: Offboarding deprovisioning exposes the limits of SSO-only control

records.applicability: D2 counterargument nuance. The benefit of rolling out Keystone over the status quo is real but partial. It also shows why SCIM reliability (C3, provisioner-v2 untested) matters, since a faulty provisioner would undermine the very deprovisioning benefit that justifies a fast rollout.
records.limitations: Vendor and community blogs (SaaS-management vendors have a commercial interest). Snippets only. Qualitative.

records.claim: The Verizon 2025 DBIR reports that compromised or stolen credentials were an initial access vector in 22% of breaches reviewed, the top vector, ahead of vulnerability exploitation (20%) and phishing (about 15-16%; sources differ). Credentials were reportedly involved in 88% of basic web application attack breaches, and infostealer logs contained company credentials for 30% of corporate-managed and 46% of unmanaged devices.

source.title: Additional 2025 DBIR research on credential stuffing

records.applicability: D2. If the status quo relies on per-application passwords without central MFA, deferral prolongs exposure to the most common breach entry vector. This weighs against an open-ended deferral and favours a time-boxed conditional or staged approach. The same statistic also shows why an IdP with unrate-limited OTP (BW-11) and untested session handling concentrates risk.
records.limitations: The 22% headline figure is from the Verizon snippet. The 88% and infostealer figures come from secondary summaries (Flare). WebFetch of www.verizon.com failed (host not allowed), so the report was not inspected. The search found no specific password-reuse or credential-stuffing percentage. Not specific to this organisation (E17). Phishing percentage differs across sources (15% vs 16%).
